items.title: This Isn’t a Landfill
items.targetTitle: The Compactor Room Is Not a Magic Hole
items.anchor: why the compactor room is not a magic hole
items.insertedSentence: I have written more about that same habit in [why the compactor room is not a magic hole](/blog/why-your-building-garbage-compactor-matters).
items.currentContent:
I have pulled a full-size metal bed frame out of a compactor chute.

I have found carpet jammed so far in that it took two of us and a good chunk of the morning to deal with it.

I have seen a broken wooden bookshelf treated like regular garbage because someone decided the chute was easier than arranging bulk pickup.

If you work in a multi-residential building, you already know the feeling. You open the garbage room door and immediately think, *not again.*

Compactor misuse never disappears completely. But there is a big difference between an occasional problem and a building where the garbage room becomes a weekly disaster. That difference usually comes down to whether anyone is actually managing it.

## A damaged compactor is not a small problem

When the compactor goes down, the whole building feels it.

Garbage starts backing up. Residents complain. Staff have to manage overflow. Vendors get called. If the machine needs parts, now you are waiting. If it happens on a Friday, good luck enjoying your weekend.

The repair bill is only one part of it.

There is also the safety side. Sharp metal, wood, carpet, Christmas trees, and oversized items do not belong in that machine. Someone eventually has to clear the jam, and that someone is usually building staff or a vendor. I am not interested in anyone getting cut, crushed, or hurt because a resident did not want to follow the bulk item process.

## Some residents honestly do not know

Not every misuse case is malicious.

Some people move in and nobody explains the garbage room. They see a chute, they see a machine, and they assume it takes everything. They do not know where bulk items go. They do not know who to call. They do not know cardboard has to be broken down.

That part is fixable.

A simple move-in sheet helps. Nothing fancy. What goes in the chute. What goes to bulk pickup. What never goes in the compactor. Who to call. Where to put large items. If your building has multiple languages, make it visual too.

You cannot expect people to follow a process nobody explained.

## The signs have to be impossible to miss

A tiny faded sign near the door does not count.

If the problem happens at the chute, put the message at the chute. Eye level. Plain language. Big enough to read. Specific examples.

"No large items" is too vague.

"No metal, wood, carpet, mattresses, furniture, electronics, paint, or Christmas trees" is better.

Pictures help too. A photo of a jammed compactor gets the point across faster than a paragraph, especially in a building where not everyone reads English comfortably.

The sign should interrupt the bad habit right before it happens.

## Cameras changed the behaviour

A camera in the garbage room made a real difference where I work.

It did not solve everything. Nothing does. But large item dumping dropped once people knew there was a record.

It also gave me something concrete when a problem happened. If I find a carpet jammed into the chute on Tuesday morning, I am not guessing. I can review footage, identify the unit, and follow up properly.

That matters because notices without proof are weak. Documentation gives the process teeth.

## Follow-through is where buildings fail

A lot of buildings do the easy part. They put up signs. They send a memo. They tell residents not to misuse the compactor.

Then someone ignores all of it and nothing happens.

Residents notice that. They learn very quickly whether the rule is real or just paper.

If a unit is confirmed dumping large items or damaging equipment, document it. Create the work order. Save photos. Issue the proper notice. Escalate through the right process if it repeats.

You do not need to be aggressive. You need to be consistent.

## Make the right option easier

If bulk pickup is hard to understand, people will use the wrong option.

Put the bulk item instructions where the problem happens. Add a phone number. Add a QR code if your building uses one. Explain whether it is free. Explain where items go and when.

Remove the excuse before it becomes one.

## The goal is fewer bad mornings

There is no perfect fix.

Some residents will still do whatever they want. New people move in. Old habits come back. Staff get busy. Signs get ignored.

But consistent signage, cameras, move-in instructions, real follow-up, and an easy bulk pickup process make a difference. I have seen it.

The goal is not a perfect garbage room. The goal is fewer jams, fewer repair calls, fewer angry residents, and fewer mornings where staff start the day pulling something out of a machine it never should have entered.

That is a win in my books.

items.title: I Pushed My Running Plan Too Fast
items.targetTitle: One Kilometre at a Time: What a Knee Injury Taught Me About Coming Back to Running
items.anchor: coming back from a knee injury one kilometre at a time
items.insertedSentence: That lesson came back later when I was [coming back from a knee injury one kilometre at a time](/blog/coming-back-to-running-after-knee-injury).
items.currentContent:
I had a plan.

That is the annoying part. I was not just winging it. I had an 11-week plan to get back to 5K. Slow build. Rest days. Easy runs. Nothing dramatic.

Then I started feeling good and decided I was smarter than the plan.

Two weeks in, I was already running 4K. My brain immediately went, look at that, I am ahead. Maybe I do not need to move so slowly. Maybe I can push this a bit.

My knees had a different opinion.

## Feeling good is not the same as being ready

This is where I messed up.

My breathing felt fine. My motivation was high. I could finish the distance. So I assumed my body was ready for more.

But running is not only lungs.

Your joints, tendons, ligaments, and smaller stabilizing muscles need time. They do not adapt as fast as your cardio. You can feel strong and still be putting stress on parts of your body that are not ready yet.

That is exactly what I did.

Both knees started getting sore. Then the soreness stuck around. Then I had to stop running completely, which is the opposite of progress.

## Skipping steps usually looks smart at first

This happens at work too.

A new person learns a task quickly and starts skipping parts of the process because it feels repetitive. Maybe nothing bad happens the first few times. That is how the bad habit gets confidence.

Then something goes wrong.

A valve was not checked. A note was not entered. A contractor was not confirmed. A small warning sign was ignored because everything seemed fine yesterday.

The process usually exists because someone learned the hard way.

That is what my running plan was. A process. I treated it like a suggestion.

## Rest days are not wasted days

I used to look at rest days like empty space.

If I felt good, why not run? Why sit around when I could get ahead?

That thinking is what got me hurt. Rest is not a break from training. It is part of the training. That is when your body catches up to the work.

The same is true in a hands-on job. You can push through for a while, but if you ignore every warning sign, eventually your body makes the decision for you.

I know that. I still had to relearn it.

## Discipline is not always pushing harder

This one stung a bit.

I like effort. I like seeing progress. I like feeling like I am doing more than expected.

But discipline is not only going hard. Sometimes discipline is stopping when the plan says stop. Running the shorter distance even though you feel like you could do more. Taking the rest day even though you are restless.

That kind of restraint is harder for me than pushing.

Anyone can get excited for a couple of weeks. The real work is staying patient long enough to keep going.

## Where I am now

I had to back off.

Ice, stretching, easier movement, no pretending the knee pain was nothing. When I get back to the plan, I am not restarting from where my ego wants me to be. I am restarting from where my body actually is.

That is frustrating, but it is better than turning a small injury into a long one.

The goal was never to prove I could run 4K in two weeks. The goal was to build a habit and get to 5K without wrecking myself.

I lost sight of that.

## The building lesson in all of this

The funny thing is, I already know this lesson from work.

When you rush a building job, it usually comes back to bite you. Skip the photos, and later nobody remembers what the problem looked like before the repair. Skip the note in the work order, and the next person has no history. Skip the small inspection because everything seems fine, and then you are surprised when the bigger issue shows up on a Friday afternoon.

The boring steps protect you.

That is what the running plan was doing. It was protecting me from myself. I just did not want to hear it because I felt good in the moment.

There is a certain kind of confidence that is useful. Then there is the kind that makes you ignore the checklist. I crossed into the second one.

## What I would tell myself now

Stick to the plan when it feels too easy.

That is probably when you need it most.

If you are building a fitness habit, learning a skill, or taking on something new at work, do not confuse early progress with readiness. Early progress feels good. It is also where a lot of people get careless.

Slow is annoying.

Starting over is worse.

items.title: One Kilometre at a Time: What a Knee Injury Taught Me About Coming Back to Running
items.targetTitle: I Pushed My Running Plan Too Fast
items.anchor: what happened when I pushed my running plan too fast
items.insertedSentence: I had already learned some of that the hard way when I wrote about [what happened when I pushed my running plan too fast](/blog/why-following-the-plan-actually-matters).
items.currentContent:
I went back out today.

One kilometre. Walked the whole thing. Didn't run a single step. And honestly? It felt like a bigger deal than it probably should have.

A month ago I tweaked my knee badly enough that I had to stop running completely. Not the kind of discomfort you push through. The kind that tells you to sit down and stay there for a while. So I did. I stayed off it, let it rest, and spent more time than I'd like to admit thinking about what I did wrong to get there in the first place.

Today was day one of getting back.

## Why I Walked Instead of Running

Here's the thing. My instinct the moment I felt a bit better was to just go. Get out there, pick up where I left off, run a few kilometres and prove to myself I was fine. That's what I would have done a year ago. And that's probably how I ended up hurt in the first place.

This time I made myself walk it. One kilometre, comfortable pace, paid attention to how the knee felt the whole way. No run, no push, no "just a little further." I've read enough about return-to-running protocols to know that the first day back should feel almost embarrassingly easy. If you come home feeling like you did something, you did too much.

I came home feeling fine. That was the goal.

## The Mistake I Keep Making

I've been running for a few years now. Not competitively, just for myself. It clears my head, gets me outside, and I genuinely love it. But I have a habit of ramping up too fast when things are going well. I'll have a good week, feel strong, and add distance before my body has actually adapted to what I'm already doing.

I've done it more than once. I did it this time.

The week before the injury I was feeling good and pushed a longer run than I should have, on tired legs, without enough of a warmup. The knee let me know pretty quickly that it wasn't happy. I kept going anyway. That part was dumb.

Looking back, there were signs I brushed off. Some stiffness in the mornings. A little ache on the outside of the knee that I told myself was just normal soreness. It wasn't. I ignored signals that were worth paying attention to.

## What a Month Off Actually Teaches You

Being forced off running for a month is frustrating. I won't pretend otherwise. But it did give me time to think about my relationship with the whole thing. Why I run, how I run, and what I want to get out of it long-term.

I don't want to be sidelined for a month every year because I keep repeating the same pattern. That's not sustainable. And if I'm being honest with myself, impatience is the thing that's gotten me hurt more than anything else. Not bad shoes, not bad form, not bad luck. Impatience.

I've seen this in other areas of life too. You skip the boring foundation work because you want to get to the good part. And then the thing you built on shaky ground falls apart and you're back at square one anyway. You might as well have taken your time the first time.

That's where I am now. Back at square one, and actually okay with it.

## The Plan Going Forward

I'm not following a rigid program I found online. But I do have a rough framework in my head. Walk for the first few days, no pressure, just get the legs used to moving again and see how the knee responds. If things stay quiet, I'll introduce short run intervals mixed in with walking. Short. Not the distance I was doing before, not even close. The kind of distance that feels almost pointless.

I'll build from there. Slowly. Slower than I want to.

I'm also going to be more honest with myself about what my legs are telling me. Stiffness that doesn't go away after a warmup is worth noting. Pain that shows up during a run and doesn't fade is worth stopping for. These aren't signs of weakness. They're information. I just have to be willing to listen to it.

## Today Was Enough

One kilometre. Walked. Knee felt fine. That's it.

No dramatic comeback story yet. No impressive splits or distance milestones. Just a guy in his neighbourhood, taking it easy, trying to do this right for once.

I'll take it.

If you're coming back from something similar and you're tempted to skip the boring early steps, I get it. But the boring early steps are the whole point. The goal isn't to run today. The goal is to still be running a year from now.

Walk the kilometre. It counts.

items.anchor: what this job is really like in subsidized housing
items.insertedSentence: It is one of those parts of [what this job is really like in subsidized housing](/blog/not-all-heroes-wear-capes-superintendent-subsidized-housing-toronto) that does not fit neatly into a work order.
items.currentContent:
I want to be straightforward about something before I get into this: I don't enjoy this part of the job. Not because I have any sympathy for what happened here, but because the whole situation is a reminder of how badly this system can be abused, and how long it can go on before anyone catches it.

We're in the middle of an eviction process right now. The tenant, who I'll call Margaret, has been living in a rent-geared-to-income unit in this building for several years. Her rent was calculated based on her reported income. She went through the standard review process. On paper, she looked eligible.

She wasn't.

## How These Things Surface

RGI eligibility isn't a one-time thing. It's reviewed periodically. Tenants are required to report their household income, assets, and composition on a regular basis, and that information gets checked against what's on record. The process exists precisely because people's circumstances change, and the subsidy is supposed to reflect what someone actually needs, not what they reported years ago.

In Margaret's case, the review flagged inconsistencies. When the records were cross-checked through the verification process, it came out that she owns multiple properties. Not vacant land. Not an inherited property sitting empty somewhere. Occupied properties, generating rental income, with tenants living in them.

That's not a grey area. That is a direct violation of RGI eligibility rules. You cannot own occupied residential properties and receive rent-geared-to-income housing assistance. The rules are explicit. She knew them, or she should have known them, because every tenant signs off on understanding them as a condition of the subsidy.

## What the Verification Process Actually Looks Like

I'm not involved in the income verification side of this directly. That's handled at a higher level, through the organization's housing eligibility team. But what I understand from having seen a few of these cases over the years is that it typically involves cross-referencing a tenant's declarations against things like property assessment records, income tax filings, and other public or administrative data sources. It's not foolproof, and it doesn't happen in real time, which is part of why someone can slip through for a long time before it catches up with them.

The periodic review process is the checkpoint. And when that checkpoint works the way it's supposed to, this is what happens: the discrepancy surfaces, it gets investigated, and if the investigation confirms what the records suggest, the file moves toward the housing tribunal.

That's where Margaret's case is now. It's a formal process with its own timeline, and I'm not going to get into the procedural details here. But the outcome, assuming nothing changes, is that she'll be losing this unit.

## The Part That Actually Bothers Me

There is a waitlist for RGI housing in this city. It is not a short one. People wait years. Some of them are living in genuinely precarious situations right now: couch surfing, sharing one-bedroom apartments with extended family, paying rent that takes up more than half of a modest income, aging out of situations that aren't sustainable. These are people who filled out the paperwork, told the truth, and got put in a queue.

Margaret was not in that queue. Margaret was collecting rent from tenants in her own properties while paying subsidized rent here. The math on that is uncomfortable to think about for too long.

I've seen a few eligibility cases over the years, but this one is about as clear-cut as it gets. There's no ambiguity about what the rules say. There's no unusual hardship being overlooked by a rigid policy. She owns income-producing properties. She was receiving a housing subsidy meant for people who own nothing and have nowhere else to go.

That's what makes this different from other compliance situations. Most tenant issues involve some degree of context, some nuance. Someone struggling with a hoarding situation, someone dealing with mental health challenges that affect how they interact with neighbours, a household that grew beyond the unit's capacity because of a family emergency. Those cases are complicated. You hold two things in mind at once.

This case doesn't ask me to do that.

## Where Things Stand

The file is with the team handling the tribunal process. My role right now is mostly administrative on the building side: making sure the work order documentation is in order, being available if anything comes up operationally, and preparing for what comes after.

What comes after is someone else getting this unit. Someone who's been waiting. Someone for whom this is not a backup plan.

That's the part I keep coming back to. Not Margaret's situation, but whoever is next on that list. They don't know yet that something shifted. But eventually this unit gets freed up and offered to someone who genuinely needs it, and that's the only part of this whole thing that feels right.

She wasn't.

## How These Things Surface

RGI eligibility isn't a one-time thing. It's reviewed periodically. This case doesn't ask me to do that.

items.title: Mould Starts Small, Then It Becomes Everyone’s Problem
items.targetTitle: At Least Three Townhouse Basements Flooded in One Morning
items.anchor: what happened when townhouse basements flooded after heavy rain
items.insertedSentence: The same moisture worry was in my head when [townhouse basements flooded after heavy rain](/blog/basement-flooding-old-townhouses).
items.currentContent:
Mould usually starts quietly.

A bit of black around the bathtub. A musty smell in a bedroom. Condensation on the window every morning. A patch near the ceiling that someone keeps wiping but it keeps coming back.

That is the part people miss. Mould is not the main problem at first. Moisture is.

If you do not deal with the moisture, the mould comes back. You can scrub it, spray it, paint over it, pretend it is gone, and it will still come back if the wall stays damp or the room has no airflow.

I have seen this enough times in buildings to know the pattern.

## First question: where is the water coming from?

Before anyone starts cleaning, you need to find the source.

Is there a leak behind the wall? Is the bathroom fan working? Is the tenant drying clothes inside with no ventilation? Is the window sweating every day? Is there water coming from the roof, the unit above, or a pipe chase?

You cannot fix mould properly if you skip that question.

Sometimes the answer is obvious. A leaking pipe under a sink. A bathroom with no fan. A basement wall that gets damp every time it rains.

Sometimes it takes more looking. You may need to check plumbing, exterior walls, window seals, exhaust fans, or past water damage.

But the source matters. Cleaning without fixing moisture is just buying time.

## Small patches are different from serious mould

A small patch on a bathroom surface can often be cleaned safely with proper protection and the right product. Gloves, mask, ventilation, clean the surface, dry it properly, and keep an eye on it.

But large areas are different. Mould inside walls is different. Mould that keeps coming back after cleaning is different. Mould after flooding is different.

That is when you stop treating it like a weekend cleaning job and bring in the right people.

I know nobody wants to hear that because professional remediation costs money. But so does ignoring it. By the time mould gets into drywall, insulation, flooring, or cabinets, the repair becomes much bigger than a surface clean.

## Health matters, especially for vulnerable people

Some people can be around a small amount of mould and only get mild irritation. Other people cannot.

Kids, seniors, people with asthma, allergies, breathing issues, or weaker immune systems can react badly. Coughing, headaches, irritated eyes, sinus problems, asthma flare-ups. I have had enough tenant conversations about this to take it seriously.

You do not need to panic every time you see a dark spot. But you should not ignore it either.

If someone in the unit is already having breathing issues, treat the problem with more urgency.

## Ventilation is not optional

Bathrooms are the big one.

People take long hot showers, close the door, leave the fan off, and wonder why the ceiling gets stained. Moisture needs somewhere to go. If it stays in the room, it lands on cold surfaces and feeds the problem.

Use the fan. Leave it running after the shower. Open the door when you can. Wipe down wet areas if the bathroom has poor airflow. Do not leave wet towels piled in a corner.

None of that sounds exciting, but it works.

The same goes for kitchens, bedrooms with condensation, and basements. Air movement matters. Humidity matters. Dry surfaces matter.

## Do not paint over it and call it fixed

This drives me crazy.

Painting over mould without fixing the moisture is like putting a clean shirt over a dirty wound. It might look better for a while, but the problem is still there.

If the surface is contaminated, clean it properly first. If the material is damaged, remove and replace it. If the source of moisture is active, fix that before finishing the wall.

Otherwise you will be back in the same spot later, usually with a bigger repair.

## Prevention is mostly boring habits

Keep indoor humidity under control. Use bathroom and kitchen fans. Report leaks early. Do not block vents. Keep furniture a little away from cold exterior walls if condensation is a problem. Dry wet areas quickly. After a flood or leak, do not assume it will dry on its own behind the baseboard.

That last one is important.

Water hides. It gets under flooring, behind trim, inside cabinets, and into drywall. The surface can look dry while the material behind it is still damp.

That is how mould gets ahead of you.

## The honest version

Mould is not always a disaster. Sometimes it is a small maintenance issue caught early.

But it becomes a bigger problem when people wait, hide it, paint over it, or clean only the visible part while leaving the moisture alone.

If you see it, deal with it early. If you smell it, look for it. If it keeps coming back, stop guessing and find the source.

That is the difference between a small fix and a problem that spreads.

items.title: What Actually Happens When You Report a Leaky Faucet

items.insertedSentence: This is exactly why I keep saying that [reporting building issues clearly matters](/blog/no-i-cant-read-your-mind-why-reporting-building-issues-matters).
items.currentContent:
A dripping faucet is one of those calls that sounds small.

Sometimes it is small. Tighten this, replace that, test it, clean up, close the work order.

Other times, the tenant says "it drips a little" and you walk in to find water running under the sink, a shut-off valve that does not fully shut, and a cabinet floor already starting to swell. That is why I do not like guessing from the hallway.

You have to look at it properly.

## The work order matters

The first part is not the tool bag. It is the work order.

I want the unit number, the date, what the tenant reported, and whether there is active leaking. If there is water escaping and causing damage, that jumps ahead of a slow drip. That is not being dramatic. Water can ruin flooring, cabinets, drywall, and the unit below if you leave it long enough.

A good work order also protects everyone later. If the same faucet keeps failing, the history is there. If a tenant says nobody came, the record is there. If the fixture needs replacement instead of another small repair, the pattern is there.

Documentation is boring until you need it.

## First look: where is the water actually coming from?

When I get into the unit, I do not start taking things apart right away.

I run the faucet. I look under the sink. I check the handles, the base, the spout, the supply lines, and the shut-off valves. I ask the tenant when it happens. Only when hot water runs? Only when the handle is turned a certain way? All the time, even when it is off?

That tells you a lot.

A drip from the spout might be a cartridge or washer. Water around the base could be an O-ring. Water under the sink could be a supply line, drain issue, or loose connection. Low pressure might be as simple as a clogged aerator.

The repair depends on the source. Guessing wastes time.

## Shut the water before you get brave

Before anything comes apart, the water gets shut off.

Under-sink valves are supposed to make this easy. Sometimes they do. Sometimes they are stiff, seized, leaking, or so old you do not trust them. If I am not confident the valve is holding, I stop and deal with that first.

There is no prize for flooding a unit because you wanted to move fast.

I put a towel or small bucket under the work area, release the pressure, and check again that the water is actually off. Then the faucet can come apart.

## Parts are the real headache

People think the hard part is the repair. A lot of the time, the hard part is getting the right part.

Moen, Delta, older no-name fixtures, cartridges that look almost the same but are not, handles with hidden screws, worn stems, missing caps. If you have worked in older buildings, you know the fun.

I like to take a photo of what comes out, especially if I need to match it at a supplier. Keeping common washers, O-rings, aerators, and cartridges on hand saves a lot of trips, but you will still run into fixtures that make you shake your head.

That is building maintenance. Half skill, half detective work.

## Fix it, then test it like you do not trust it

Once the part is replaced or cleaned, I reassemble everything and turn the water back on slowly.

Then I test it.

Hot. Cold. Full pressure. Low pressure. Handle on. Handle off. Look under the sink again. Dry the area, wait a minute, check for new moisture. Sometimes a leak only shows itself after pressure comes back into the line.

If it still drips, you do not just shrug and leave. You go back in and figure out what you missed.

The tenant does not care that you tried. They care that it stopped leaking.

## Clean up before you leave

This part matters more than some people think.

Do not leave old washers, wet paper towel, packaging, or dirty fingerprints around the sink. Wipe the area. Put the tools away. Let the tenant know what was done and what to watch for.

If the faucet is old and likely to fail again, I note that too. Sometimes the honest answer is not another repair. Sometimes it is replacement.

## A small repair is still part of a bigger system

A faucet call is not glamorous. Nobody writes a thank-you card because the bathroom sink stopped dripping.

But these small calls are the job. They prevent water damage, keep tenants from getting frustrated, and show whether the building is being looked after properly.

If you are a tenant, report the leak early. Do not wait until the cabinet is soaked.

If you are a new super, slow down enough to diagnose it right. The fastest repair is the one you only have to do once.

items.title: Elevator Problems Start With Small Habits
items.targetTitle: Someone Was Urinating in the Stairwell
items.anchor: why shared spaces need basic respect
items.insertedSentence: It connects to the same basic idea I wrote about in [why shared spaces need basic respect](/blog/respecting-shared-space).
items.currentContent:
I have a soft spot for elevators because I know how much people depend on them.

Most residents do not think about the elevator until it is slow, dirty, stuck, or out of service. Fair enough. Nobody wakes up in the morning excited to appreciate the elevator. You press the button, you wait, you get in, you go upstairs. That is how it should feel.

But when it goes wrong, the whole building feels it.

If you are young and healthy, stairs are annoying. If you are elderly, using a walker, pushing a stroller, carrying groceries, or dealing with an injury, stairs can turn into a real problem fast. That is why I get a little frustrated when people treat the elevator like it is indestructible.

It is not.

## Let people get off first

This one sounds too simple to even write down, but it happens all the time.

The doors open and someone is already standing right in the middle, trying to rush in before anyone can step out. Then everyone does that awkward little shuffle where nobody can move properly. It saves no time. It just makes people irritated.

Stand to the side. Let people out. Then get in.

That tiny bit of patience makes the elevator move smoother for everyone.

## Stop holding the door forever

I am not saying never hold the door. If someone is a few steps away with their hands full, of course, hold it.

What causes problems is when someone holds the door while another person is still down the hallway, still looking for keys, still finishing a phone call, or still deciding if they are coming. Meanwhile the elevator is stuck, other floors are waiting, and the doors keep fighting against being forced open.

Those doors are not just doors. They are part of a system with sensors, rollers, tracks, motors, and controls. Keep forcing them and eventually something wears out or goes out of adjustment.

Then everyone complains that the elevator is broken.

## Report the weird stuff early

If the elevator makes a new grinding sound, bangs harder than usual, levels badly at the floor, or the doors start reversing for no clear reason, report it.

Do not wait until it fully breaks.

I would rather get a boring report early than an emergency call later. A strange sound might be nothing. It might also be the first sign that a part is wearing out or the door operator needs adjustment. Building staff cannot fix or call in what nobody reports.

A quick message can save a full shutdown.

## Do not overload it

People see a packed elevator and still try to squeeze in.

I get it. Nobody wants to wait. But if the car is full, it is full. Overloading the elevator is uncomfortable for people inside and hard on the equipment. It also makes the ride slower because the doors take longer, people have to shift around, and the elevator may not operate properly if the weight limit is pushed.

Waiting one extra trip is annoying. Getting stuck because everyone tried to force it is worse.

## Keep it clean because someone else has to touch it

Coffee spills. Garbage. Mud. Leaking grocery bags. Food smells. I have seen all of it.

People forget that elevators are small rooms everyone shares. If you leave a mess in there, someone else has to ride with it, clean it, or both. Usually it is building staff cleaning it, and it is usually during a morning when we already have ten other things waiting.

I am not asking anyone to polish the walls. Just do not leave garbage behind. If something spills, report it. If your boots are covered in mud, maybe wipe them before tracking it through the whole building.

That is not fancy etiquette. That is basic respect.

## Management has a part too

Residents are not the only ones responsible. Building management has to keep up with inspections, service calls, cleaning, and clear communication.

If the elevator is always dirty, always breaking down, or nobody explains what is going on during an outage, residents lose patience. I understand that. People deserve updates, especially when accessibility is affected.

But residents can help by using the elevator properly and reporting problems before they turn into bigger ones.

It works both ways.

## The building feels different when people care

You can tell when people respect a shared space.

The elevator is cleaner. People move aside. Nobody jams the doors open for five minutes. Weird noises get reported. Staff can deal with small problems before they become big ones.

It is not dramatic. It is not some big community project. It is just small habits repeated every day.

That is the part people underestimate. A building does not usually get better from one huge announcement. It gets better when enough people stop treating shared spaces like someone else’s problem.

That is how buildings run better. Not perfectly. Better.

And honestly, better is a good start.

items.currentContent:
I've had this conversation more times than I can count. Tenant stops me in the hallway, frustrated, and says something like, "The shower's been barely trickling for three weeks." And my first question, every single time, is the same: "Did you put in a work order?"

Silence. Sometimes a shrug. Sometimes a "I figured someone would notice."

Here's the thing, I genuinely wish I could notice everything. I walk this building every day. I pay attention. But I am not psychic, and neither is any other super or property manager you'll ever meet. We can't fix what we don't know is broken.

## The Building Is Bigger Than You Think

From the outside, a residential building looks pretty simple. People live there, stuff breaks, someone fixes it. But on the inside, it's a small city. Dozens or hundreds of units, mechanical rooms, common areas, rooftop equipment, underground parking, laundry rooms, elevators. The list goes on.

I'm moving constantly. And I'm prioritizing based on what's been reported, what's urgent, and what the schedule looks like that day. If your shower head is clogged or your smoke detector is chirping, that information has to come from you. It doesn't float up to me through the walls.

What I tell tenants is simple: you are the first line of awareness in your own unit. You live there. You notice things before anyone else possibly could.

## A Small Problem Left Unreported Becomes a Big Problem Fast

This is where I see the real cost of waiting. Had a situation once where a slow drip under a bathroom vanity went unreported for over a month. By the time it came in as a work order, the cabinet floor had rotted through and there was moisture creeping into the subfloor. What would have been a washer replacement turned into a full vanity swap and subfloor repair. Not cheap. Not fast.

Water is the enemy in any building. It doesn't take much, and it doesn't wait around while you decide if it's "worth mentioning." Same goes for a beeping smoke detector. I know the chirp is annoying, especially at 2am. But that chirp is a low battery warning, and a smoke detector with a dead battery is just a plastic disc on your ceiling. It's not protecting anyone.

Report it. I'll get it handled. That's literally what I'm here for.

## What Actually Happens When You Submit a Work Order

A lot of tenants don't realize there's a real process behind that form or that phone call. When you submit a work order, a few things happen immediately. The issue gets logged with a timestamp. It gets assigned. It creates a paper trail.

That last part matters more than people think. If the same issue keeps coming back, that history helps us figure out why. A toilet that's been rebuilt three times in two years is telling us something. Without the records, we're just guessing.

The work order also protects you as a tenant. If there's ever a question about whether something was reported, or when, or what was done about it, that record is the answer. In my experience, the tenants who submit work orders consistently are also the ones who have the smoothest experience in the building. Not a coincidence.

## How to Report an Issue So It Actually Gets Fixed

Being specific helps enormously. "My shower is broken" and "my shower has low hot water pressure, but cold pressure seems fine" are two very different starting points. The second one already tells me something useful before I even walk through the door.

Note when it started if you can. Mention if it's getting worse. If it's a noise, try to describe it, grinding, rattling, beeping, hissing. These details cut down on diagnostic time and get you to a resolution faster.

And if it's urgent, say so. A no-heat situation in February is not the same priority level as a squeaky cabinet hinge. Don't bury that information. Lead with it.

## The Communication Goes Both Ways

I'll be straight with you, building staff should also be communicating back. If a repair is going to take longer than expected, you deserve to know that. If we need to access your unit, you should get proper notice. That's part of the deal too.

But the starting point, the thing that kicks off the whole process, has to come from you. No report means no record. No record means no action. And meanwhile, the drip keeps dripping.

You don't need to apologize for reporting something. You're not bothering anyone. This is exactly what the system is built for.

## What I would do
Next time something feels off in your unit, a weird sound, a slow drain, a light that keeps flickering, don't wait to see if it resolves itself. Submit the work order today. Call the office. Send the email. Whatever your building's process is, use it.

Because the fastest path to a fixed problem always starts with someone saying, "Hey, here's what's going on." That someone has to be you.

items.title: The Compactor Room Is Not a Magic Hole
items.anchor: the ongoing battles with garbage compactor misuse
items.insertedSentence: I went deeper into the same pattern in [the ongoing battles with garbage compactor misuse](/blog/this-isn-t-a-landfill-ongoing-battles-with-garbage-compactor-misuse-in-residential-buildings).
items.currentContent:
Most tenants do not think about the compactor room unless something smells bad or the machine is down.

Honestly, that is normal. When the compactor is working, it should be boring. You bring your garbage down, toss the bag where it belongs, and leave.

But when it stops working, everyone notices fast.

Bags pile up. The room starts to smell. People leave garbage in places it should not be. Staff get pulled away from other work. Vendors have to be called. Residents start asking why nobody is doing anything, even though the whole problem may have started because someone put the wrong thing into the machine.

The compactor room is not a magic hole. What goes in there matters.

## What the compactor is actually doing

A residential building produces a lot of garbage every day.

The compactor crushes that waste down so it takes up less space and can be hauled away properly. Without it, garbage rooms fill up quickly. In the summer, that becomes a smell problem. Then a pest problem. Then a complaint problem.

I have seen compactor rooms go downhill fast when the machine is out of service. It does not take long.

That is why staff care about how residents use it. We are not being picky for fun. We are trying to keep the building running.

## The biggest problems are preventable

Most compactor headaches come from the same things.

Cardboard that was not broken down. Loose bags leaking down the chute. Food waste not tied properly. Furniture pieces. Metal. Wood. Electronics. Paint cans. Construction debris. Stuff that should have gone to bulk pickup or hazardous waste.

Some of it jams the chute. Some of it damages the machine. Some of it creates smells. Some of it is just dangerous.

And once the machine starts struggling, small problems become expensive ones.

A jam caught early might be manageable. A jam ignored until the motor keeps fighting against it can turn into a real repair.

## Tie the bag

This might be the simplest thing in the whole post.

Tie your garbage bag.

If liquid leaks down the chute, it does not magically disappear. It sits. It smells. It feeds bacteria. It makes the room worse for everyone and creates more cleaning work for staff.

Same with loose food, broken glass, or sharp items. Bag it properly. If it should not go in regular garbage, do not put it there.

That one habit prevents a lot of mess.

## Large items do not belong there

If you bought a couch, a bed frame, a TV stand, or anything with big packaging, do not try to make the compactor deal with it.

Break down what can be broken down. Use the recycling area if your building has one. For furniture, mattresses, wood, metal, and other bulky items, follow the bulk pickup process.

If you are not sure, ask.

I would rather answer a thirty-second question than spend two hours dealing with a jammed chute.

That is not an exaggeration. One wrong item can block the chute for multiple floors. Then residents keep trying to use it because they do not know it is blocked, and now the mess stacks up above the original problem. By the time staff find it, the fix is no longer quick.

This is why I care about boring things like cardboard, bag size, and whether people read the sign. Boring things are usually what keep the building from becoming chaotic.

## Staff need to maintain it too

Residents have responsibilities, but building staff and management do too.

The room needs clear signage. New residents need instructions. The machine needs regular service. Chutes need cleaning. Drains need attention. Staff should know the warning signs: strange noises, repeated cycling, weak compression, leaks, or garbage backing up.

You cannot ignore the machine for months and then act surprised when it fails.

Good maintenance and good resident habits have to work together.

## Cameras help, but they are not the whole answer

A camera in the compactor room can help with accountability. People behave differently when they know there is a record, and staff can follow up when someone dumps the wrong thing.

But cameras do not replace communication.

If residents do not know the rules, teach them. If the signs are old and useless, replace them. If bulk pickup exists, make the process easy to find.

The goal is not to catch everyone. The goal is to reduce the problem.

## One quick check

If you manage a building, go look at your compactor room today.

Is the signage clear? Does it say exactly what cannot go in? Is the bulk pickup information posted where residents can see it? Does the room smell worse than it should? Is the machine making sounds it did not make before?

If you are a tenant, read the sign next time you are there. Tie your bags. Do not force large items into a system that was never built for them.

A working compactor is one of those things nobody appreciates until it is down.

Trust me, you want it boring.
